pass_a_gloss: [...] and arbiter and teacher Christ himself has become for us. And someone would say that mercy and righteousness rising from earth, or also having sprouted, is our Lord Jesus the Christ himself. For he has become for us from God and Father mercy and righteousness; if indeed it is true that we were pitied in him, and have been justified, having received the forgiveness of the ancient accusations, or that from him we have received the righteousness able to bring us back into the lot of every good, through which also we have been saved. And if the earth has been ordered to make righteousness spring up, let no one be vexed, having considered that the Psalmist too says somewhere about God and Father, and about Emmanuel himself: He worked righteousness in the middle of the earth. For not from above and out of heaven did Christ bring down to us his own flesh, but rather he was born according to flesh from a woman, who also was one of those on earth. Whenever then it is said that he became fruit and shoot of earth, you will understand, as I said, that he came to be according to flesh from a woman taken for this toward service, although being one of those from the earth. [Lemma, Isaiah 45:8-9:] I am the Lord God, the one who created you; what sort of better thing did I construct like clay of a potter? He gives as it were in these the cause of also the Son, being God according to nature, emptying himself, and choosing also to suffer for us, and deeming those being on the earth worthy of so great sparing, as to give up his own soul as an exchange; or rather also to endure taking the form of the slave, and to exchange for the highest glory the lowliness of the nature of man. For this reason he says that, I am, now is to be taken instead of: I subsist and live, being true God, and Lord of the powers, and having brought into being all things, and not having made death, but rather having created all things for incorruption. Then honouring the nature of man, and that of all the living things on earth nothing at all would weigh equal to it, What sort, he says, of better thing did I construct like clay of a potter? For we have been formed by him having taken dust from the earth, and having shaped very well like a potter. But not as far as these is the dignity of the nature of man, but also something greater in us, a guest-gift and present of the fine craft of God. For we have been made according to his image and likeness, and we have been enriched with the stamp of his glory flashing spiritually in our souls, even if we are according to flesh earth and from earth. So not contemptible, but rather also admirable is man, a living being on earth; and thus God prides himself on him. And so he said to the most enduring Job, making his own great works clear: Or having taken clay of earth, did you form a living being, and set it speaking upon the earth? [The section breaks off.]
pass_b_english: …and arbiter and teacher, Christ Himself has become for us. One might also say that the mercy and righteousness that rises from the earth, or springs up from it (Isaiah 45:8), is our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. For He has become for us, from God the Father, mercy and righteousness (compare 1 Corinthians 1:30), since it is true that in Him we received mercy and were justified, receiving forgiveness of our old offenses; that is, from Him we have received the righteousness that can bring us to our share in every good, the righteousness by which we have also been saved.

If the earth is commanded to make righteousness spring up, let no one be annoyed, when he considers that the Psalmist too says somewhere, of God the Father and of Emmanuel Himself: “He worked righteousness in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). For Christ did not bring His own flesh down to us from above, out of heaven; rather, He was born according to the flesh of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who was herself one of those on the earth. So when He is said to have become the fruit and shoot of the earth, you will understand, as I said, that He was born according to the flesh of a woman taken for this service, though she was one of those from the earth.
“I am the Lord God, who created you. What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” (Isaiah 45:8-9).

Here He gives, as it were, the reason why the Son, though He is God by nature, emptied Himself, chose even to suffer for us, and counted those on the earth worthy of so great a care that He gave up His own life in exchange for them; or rather, why He consented to take the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and to exchange the supreme glory for the lowliness of human nature. That is why He says, “I am”; this is to be taken here in place of “I subsist and live,” since He is true God and Lord of hosts, who brought all things into being, who did not make death but rather created all things for incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13-14; 2:23).

Then, honoring human nature, and showing that of all living creatures on earth none at all could match it, He says, “What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” For we were formed by Him when He took dust from the earth (Genesis 2:7) and shaped it very well, as a potter does. Yet the dignity of human nature does not stop there; there is in us something greater still, a guest-gift and a present from God’s fine craftsmanship. For we have been made according to His image and likeness (Genesis 1:26), and we have been enriched with the stamp of His glory, shining spiritually in our souls, even though according to the flesh we are earth and from the earth.

So man is no contemptible creature, but rather a living being on earth worthy of admiration; and God takes such pride in him. Indeed He said to Job, who endured so much, when He was setting out His mighty works plainly: “Did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth able to speak?” (Job 38:14) …

choices.term: γεγένηται δὲ μᾶλλον κατὰ σάρκα ἐκ γυναικὸς
choices.english: He was born according to the flesh of a woman
choices.why: The cause of the Incarnation is given to the Son himself; the flesh comes from a woman of the earth.

choices.english: to exchange the supreme glory for the lowliness of human nature
choices.why: The Son takes human lowliness in place of his glory (Philippians 2:7).
rejected: transformed the insignificance of human nature

choices.why: Cyril takes 'I am' of God's own subsisting being.
Two words for the gift of the divine image; both are kept.
χαρακτήρ, the stamp of a seal or coin; the image shining in our souls.
